Title: A Unified Fractional Regularization Framework for Sparse Recovery
Text:
A UNIFIED FRACTIONAL REGULARIZATION FRAMEWORK FOR
SPARSE RECOVERY∗
YINHAO ZHAO†, HAOYU HE‡, CHUANQI MA§, AND HAO WANG¶
Abstract. We propose a unified fractional regularization framework for sparse signal recovery
based on the ℓ1/ℓq
p model. Our main theoretical contribution is the characterization of the equiva-
lence between the first-order stationary points of the ℓ1/ℓq
p formulation and the subtractive ℓ1 −αℓp
model, providing a unified perspective on these nonconvex regularizers. In addition, we establish a
new sufficient recovery condition under the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP), showing that the
framework’s robustness even under high-coherence sensing matrices. To solve the resulting prob-
lem, we develop a majorization–minimization (MM) algorithm and prove its convergence via the
Kurdyka– Lojasiewicz (KL) property. Numerical experiments on different sensing matrices and MRI
reconstruction demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently outperforms existing methods.
Key words.
Sparse recovery; Fractional regularization; Restricted Isometry Property; Ma-
jorization Minimization algorithm.
1. Introduction. Sparse recovery aims to find a sparse solution x ∈Rn (i.e.,
with most entries being zero) to the underdetermined linear system Ax = b, where
A ∈Rm×n is the sensing matrix and b ∈Rm is the observed signal. This problem
arises in numerous applications including compressed sensing (CS), magnetic reso-
nance imaging (MRI), and radar signal processing. The most direct formulation is
the ℓ0-norm minimization:
(1.1)
minimize
∥x∥0
subject to
Ax = b,
where ∥x∥0 = Pn
i=1 1{xi̸=0} counts the number of nonzeros. However, solving (1.1)
is NP-hard [18], rendering it computationally intractable for large-scale problems.
Consequently, a standard approach is to replace the non-convex ℓ0 norm with the
convex ℓ1 norm, leading to the Basis Pursuit (BP) problem [10]:
(1.2)
minimize
∥x∥1
subject to
Ax = b.
Extensive research has established that when the sensing matrix A satisfies the
Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) [8] and the signal x is sufficiently sparse, the ℓ1
minimizer can exactly recover x. This result has played a central role in the devel-
opment of compressed sensing and has motivated the design of efficient optimization
algorithms, such as FISTA [5] and ADMM [7].
Importantly, a broad class of random matrices, including Gaussian, sub-Gaussian,
and subsampled Fourier matrices, have been shown to satisfy the RIP with high
probability [4,20], which provides theoretical justification for their widespread use in
practical applications.

In recent years, nonconvex surrogates such as ℓp(0 < p < 1) [9] and SCAD [13]
have attracted attention for providing tighter approximations to the ℓ0 norm. Within
this context, two prominent paradigms have emerged:
(a) Subtractive Models: The ℓ1 −αℓp regularization [12,16,28], defined as:

α, one balances convexity (ℓ1 dominance when α →0+) and nonconvexity
(enhancing sparsity when α increases). Moreover, the ℓ1−αℓp model provides
an effective approach for ratio-based sparsity regularization [16].
(b) Ratio Models: The ℓ1/ℓp regularization (p > 1) [25], which is scale-invariant
and highly effective for high-dynamic signals:
(1.4)

∥x∥1

This ratio shares key sparsity-inducing properties with the ℓ0 norm. Cru-
cially, (1.4) is scale-invariant: for any β > 0,

optimization is insensitive to the magnitude of x. When p = 2, the model
simplifies to ℓ1/ℓ2, where the ratio ℓ1/ℓ2 was introduced as a sparsity measure
in [15]. Theoretical analysis shows that under a strong Null Space Property
(sNSP), sparse solutions are local minimizers of (1.4) [19].
Furthermore,
DC algorithms applied to ℓ1/ℓ2 exhibit linear convergence [26], and efficient
solvers based on ADMM, bisection, and adaptive methods have been devel-
oped [19,22–24,26].
Previous studies have explored the Null Space Property (sNSP) [19] and DC
algorithms [22–24, 26] for ratio models. Notably, Yin et al. [24] observed that (1.4)
is equivalent to (1.3) only when α is set to the specific value ∥x∗∥1/∥x∗∥p. However,
since the optimal x∗is unknown a priori, a fundamental question remains: Does a
general equivalence exist between difference-based and ratio-based regularizations for
arbitrary α > 0? Furthermore, does a unified framework exist that encompasses these
variants while providing robust RIP guarantees?
The ℓ1/ℓ2 ratio is particularly valued for its scale invariance and its close approx-
imation to the ℓ0 norm. A key insight is that ℓ1/ℓ2 regularization is asymptotically
equivalent to ℓ1 −αℓ2 regularization when the optimal solution x∗is known. Specifi-
cally, setting α∗= ∥x∗∥1/∥x∗∥2 in (1.3) yields the same global optimum as (1.4) [24].
However, this equivalence requires prior knowledge of x∗, which is unavailable in
practice.
However, a natural question arises about the regularization of the ℓ1−αℓ2 regular-
ization for more general α. Specifically, does ℓ1−αℓ2 regularization always correspond
to some form of fraction regularization, or does it lead to entirely different types of
regularization? Addressing this gap requires a deeper investigation into the structural
equivalence of these regularizations, as well as an understanding of cases where the
formulation ℓ1 −αℓ2 may lack a direct correspondence to the ℓ1/ℓ2 regularization.
While concurrent work [27] has extended ratio models to block-sparse scenarios, the
structural connection between ratio and subtraction models remains unresolved. The
resolution of this question has significant implications for the development of robust
and flexible regularization techniques for sparse signal recovery.

Our main contributions are:
1. Theoretical Equivalence. We prove that any critical point of (1.5) corresponds
to a critical point of an ℓ1 −αℓp problem for a specific α. This resolves the
open question by revealing the intrinsic link between fractional and difference-
based regularizations for arbitrary parameters.
2. Recovery Guarantee. We derive a new RIP-based condition for (1.5). This
condition is weaker than many existing nonconvex guarantees [9], ensuring
robustness even under moderate coherence.
3. Efficient MM Algorithm. We develop a tailored Majorization Minimization
(MM) algorithm with an adaptive scheme. We prove its global convergence
and local convergence rate.
4. Superior Performance.
Numerical experiments on sparse signal recovery,
time-domain signal reconstruction, and MRI reconstruction demonstrate that
the proposed ℓ1/ℓq
p model consistently outperforms the classical ℓ1, ℓ1 −ℓ2,
and ℓ1/ℓ2 models in terms of recovery accuracy.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces notation
and preliminary concepts. Section III presents the theoretical equivalence between
(1.5) and ℓ1 −αℓp regularization. Section IV provides the sufficient recovery condition
under RIP. Section IV develops our MM algorithm for solving (1.5) and establishes
its local linear convergence. Section V provides extensive numerical results comparing
our method against benchmarks. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper.

2.2. KL Properties. The Kurdyka– Lojasiewicz (KL) property is essential for
proving the convergence of descent methods for minimizing F. The convergence of
the sequence {xk} is established by verifying the standard conditions for descent
methods (see [1–3, 6]). If the descent algorithm ensures a sufficient descent of the
objective function and the subgradient is bounded by the successive iterates, satisfying
conditions H1–H3 in [3, Section 2.3]. Given the boundedness of {xk} and the fact that
the objective F is a KL function, one can invoke the KL framework to conclude that
the entire sequence {xk} converges to a stationary point of F.
Definition 2.1 (KL Property [3]). A proper lower semicontinuous function f
satisfies the KL property at ¯x ∈dom ∂f if there exist η ∈(0, +∞], a neighborhood U
of ¯x, and a concave function ϕ(s) = cs1−θ for some c > 0 and θ ∈[0, 1), such that
for all x ∈U ∩{x : f(¯x) < f(x) < f(¯x) + η}, one has
ϕ′(f(x) −f(¯x)) dist(0, ∂f(x)) ≥1.
The value θ is referred to as the KL exponent.
The KL exponent θ plays a pivotal role in determining the convergence rate of
the proposed DC algorithm. Specifically:
• If θ ∈(0, 1/2], the sequence {xk} converges to ¯x at a linear rate, i.e., ∥xk −
¯x∥≤O(ρk) for some ρ ∈(0, 1).
• If θ ∈(1/2, 1), the convergence is sublinear, satisfying ∥xk −¯x∥≤O(k−1−θ
2θ−1 ).

In our experiments, the 256 × 256 Shepp–Logan phantom is used as the ground
truth image, shown in Fig. 7.3a. The MRI sampling process is simulated using a
radial sampling pattern in the frequency domain, where five radial lines are selected,
as illustrated in Fig. 7.3b. Consistent with our constrained formulation, no additional
noise is added. The resulting optimization problem is solved using the same framework
as described in the previous sections, since the structure remains analogous after
introducing the gradient operator.
We compare the classical ℓ1 model, the ℓ1/ℓ2 model, and two variants of the
proposed ℓ1/ℓq
p formulation with parameter settings (p, q) = (2.0, 0.7) and (p, q) =
(2.5, 0.9). The reconstruction results are shown in Fig. 7.3. The classical ℓ1 model
produces severe artifacts due to the extremely limited measurements, resulting in a
high relative error of 53.86% (Fig. 7.3c). The ℓ1/ℓ2 model improves the reconstruction
quality and reduces the error to 10.30%, although visible artifacts remain (Fig. 7.3d).
In contrast, the proposed ℓ1/ℓq
p models achieve significantly better reconstructions.
The configuration (p, q) = (2.0, 0.7) reduces the relative error to 0.26% and produces
a nearly artifact-free image (Fig. 7.3e). The configuration (p, q) = (2.5, 0.9) further
improves the reconstruction quality, achieving the lowest error of 0.15% (Fig. 7.3f).
These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model for recovering struc-
tured images from highly undersampled measurements.
8. Conclusion. In this paper, we proposed a sparse signal recovery model based
on the ℓ1/ℓq
p regularization, and established its connection with the ℓ1 −αℓp formu-
lation through the equivalence of first-order stationary points. We further derived a
sufficient recovery condition under the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP), showing
that smaller values of q lead to less restrictive bounds and improved error estimates.
To solve the resulting problem, we developed an efficient majorization–minimization
(MM) algorithm and established its convergence via the Kurdyka– Lojasiewicz (KL)
property. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves su-
perior performance across a range of representative sparse recovery tasks. Although
smaller q improves theoretical recovery guarantees, it may hinder algorithmic per-
formance. Future work will aim to improve both the modeling capability and the
robustness of the optimization algorithm.

Abstract: We propose a unified fractional regularization framework for sparse signal recovery based on the ℓ1/ℓq p model. Our main theoretical contribution is the characterization of the equiva- lence between the first-order stationary points of the ℓ1/ℓq p formulation and the subtractive ℓ1 −αℓp model, providing a unified perspective on these nonconvex regularizers. In addition, we establish a new sufficient recovery condition under the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP), showing that the framework’s robustness even under high-coherence sensing matrices. To solve the resulting prob- lem, we develop a majorization–minimization (MM) algorithm and prove its convergence via the Kurdyka– Lojasiewicz (KL) property. Numerical experiments on different sensing matrices and MRI reconstruction demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently outperforms existing methods.
